title: Blended finance

definition.text: Blended finance uses public development money and charitable funds strategically to draw private investment into developing countries.

facts.text: It mixes public and private funds in one deal, each party using its expertise in a complementary way.
It aims at the Sustainable Development Goals, which in 2017 estimates needed an extra $2.5 trillion a year in financing.
Philanthropic or concessional money takes the first losses, reassuring private investors that their principal is protected.
Each concessional dollar can attract several private dollars, often 3x to 10x; a $2 million first-loss layer drawing $10 million is a 5x multiplier.
The OECD's Development Assistance Committee adopted blended finance principles in 2018.
The OECD identified 180 blended finance funds and facilities with $60.2 billion invested across 111 developing countries.
Critics say it shifts profits to private, mostly Northern, investors while leaving risks with Southern governments, and that its complexity weakens transparency.
In nature conservation it is used to overcome risk, small deal sizes and transaction costs that deter private investors.

contested_note: Scholars and NGOs criticise blended finance for shifting profits to private investors and risks to poorer countries' governments.

definition.text: Development funders support private investors in blended deals through technical assistance, risk underwriting and market incentives.

facts.text: Technical assistance uses grants to build investees' capacity and lower transaction costs.
Guarantees, insurance and concessional tranches reduce risks such as currency swings, political instability and default.
Because concessional capital is catalytic rather than continuous, it can be recycled into new projects once investors gain confidence.

definition.text: Land trusts are nonprofit or fiduciary arrangements that own and manage land, and sometimes water.

facts.text: The three common types are real estate investment trusts, community land trusts for affordable housing, and conservation land trusts.
Land trusts date back at least to Roman times, but their clearest history begins in Henry VIII's England.
In Australia, Aboriginal land trusts hold freehold title to land on behalf of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

definition.text: A catastrophe bond moves a defined disaster risk from a sponsor, usually an insurer, to investors.

facts.text: If the named disaster happens, the principal goes to the sponsor to fund recovery; otherwise investors get it back at maturity plus interest.
They were first used in the mid-1990s after Hurricane Andrew and the Northridge earthquake.
Rising climate-related disaster risk has led governments and insurers to use them when reinsurance is unavailable or too costly.
Investors like them because returns are largely uncorrelated with stocks and ordinary bonds, aiding diversification.
Swiss Re estimated the market at $43.1 billion at the end of 2023, with a record $15.4 billion issued that year.
Most are rated below investment grade, B or BB, based on the probability a qualifying disaster triggers a loss.

definition.text: Catastrophe bonds pay out under different triggers: the insurer's actual losses, modelled losses, industry-wide losses, or measured event parameters.

facts.text: Triggers closer to the insurer's own losses protect it better; index and parametric triggers spare investors from the insurer's claims handling.
A trigger can apply per single event or to the sum of losses over a period, usually a year.
Example: with a $90 billion aggregate attachment, three $20 billion hurricanes and a $40 billion earthquake total $100 billion and trigger payout.
